utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, you can have your last 13 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, did you -- did the Court want to caution the witness before we started?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much. Mr. Babic, as always, once again you are being reminded you're bound by the declaration you made to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic, can you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, what was Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Flash was a Croatian military police intervention on the territory of Western Slavonia which was held by the Serbs, at the beginning of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what if anything precipitated Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what precipitated it was, and what was the reason for the operation, were the events that took place along the motorway from Okucani on the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those events were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those events came about after a long period of negotiation between the representatives of the government of Croatia and the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina which I took part in. The negotiations went on for some months, about the normalisation of relations between the Republic of Srpska Krajina and Croatia in the sense of linking up the electrical power system and the water work system and opening up the motorway between Zagreb and Belgrade, opening the railway lines and things like that. After those talks, a portion of the agreement was realised and that was the opening of the Belgrade-Zagreb motorway across the territory which was controlled by the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and that was Western Slavonia, that area there, and a small part of Eastern Slavonia. The motorway functioned or was opened for a time until -- in 1995, until May 1995, and after the motorway was running normally, incidents took place along the motorway and it was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who closed it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as my information told me, from the Prime Minister, Mikelic, Mr. Martic, with policemen and people from the area of Okucani issued orders to close off the motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened after the motorway was closed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negotiations were conducted to discuss its reopening. However, Croatia opened the motorway by force or rather there was a military police operation, an onslaught by which it opened the motorway and took control of the territory of Western Slavonia which had hitherto been under the control of the Serbs. So those were the operations and they went on for several days, the 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd of May, in fact. Everything was over by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is that what we referred to earlier as Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Milan Martic, to your knowledge, do something after Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he -- on the second day of the -- of Operation Flash, he ordered the shelling of the town of Zagreb in retaliation for Croatia's intervention in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how do you know that he ordered it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said himself, on television, that he had issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'd like to look at intercept 593, please. And there is a beginning part there that I would like to ignore and just start with Mikelic and Milosevic, and in your declaration, you stated that you recognised the voices of Slobodan Milosevic and Borisav Mikelic. You've referred in your testimony to Borisav Mikelic. Could you remind us again who he was at that time, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borisav Mikelic was at the time the Prime Minister of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There was at the time that you yourself was in the government -- were in the government as the Minister of Foreign Affairs; is that correct? You testified about that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, in which government SAO Krajina or Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At this time it's the RSK in 1995, the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many times you had occasion to speak with Borisav Mikelic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frequently. I can't give you an exact number but over the course of two years, I was a member of the government of which he was Prime Minister, so fairly often. Sometimes daily. Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us just in general terms what this conversation is about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this conversation, they are discussing topics linked to the events which took place in Western Slavonia, and that was Martic's order of the shelling of Zagreb and the consequences thereof, what came before the event, then there is mention there about certain additional matters such as the meeting of a joint council of the supreme defence between the Republic of Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska, mention is made of the problems that the Minister of the Interior is encountering, and preparations for an assembly meeting of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. But for the most part it's all linked to this particular events in Western Slavonia and Operation Flash and the shelling of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have to pause for a moment because I lost my transcript. I just have to get it back up here. I'd like to play a clip that starts at page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. It starts with Mr. Mikelic saying, "Boro speaking." Do you see that? On page 2 of the transcript. Sorry, actually I think it's on page 1 of the B/C/S. It starts on page 1, at the bottom of page 1 of the B/C/S transcript. Do you -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could turn the Sanction on from the AV booth, please. It actually starts with, "Hello, Mr. President."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello, Mr. President, what's up?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The procedure that we agreed to yesterday with respect to this -- these transcripts and we may have to provide the B/C/S to the French booth, is that in the -- is that the English -- the interpreters do not need to read the English transcript and we'll just listen to the original.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the French booth is now being provided with the transcript in B/C/S which we should have done before we started today, and my apologies. And as soon as they have it we can start playing it. And again for the benefit of the French booth, it starts at the bottom of page 1 of the B/C/S or the top of page 2. Okay. If we could play it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in that clip, Slobodan Milosevic says, "No one doubted Tudjman's unscrupulousness even before, but if there had not been for Martic's capriciousness the road would not have been opened for his unscrupulousness. Martic's capriciousness has opened the road for the unscrupulousness of Tudjman because if he had not done that thing with the motorway, which he did and started the fires, this one would never have dared due to the international situation, to put in question a decision which has been set and sanctioned by UN regarding the regime in Western Slavonia." What do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is provocation, in fact, on the part of Martic, which took place when the motorway was closed, the violation of the agreement reached between the government of Krajina and government of Croatia under the auspices or leadership of the United Nations, who were the guarantor of that agreement. So that is the provocation. It was a provocation to close the motorway and violate the international agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when Mr. Milosevic says, "If he had not done that thing with the motorway, which he did and started the fires, this one never would never have dared." Dared do what, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To militarily attack Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play a second clip and this one begins on page 3 of the English transcript, page 2 of the B/C/S. It begins with where Mikelic says, "Martic was in Banja Luka yesterday." Now, when we listen to this clip, Mr. Babic, I'm going to ask you to listen very carefully to see if you can tell who says what in this clip. It's a little hard to hear in the courtroom. It's actually -- I can say it's easier whether we have listened to it outside the courtroom but playing it through the system in the courtroom, a little hard but I will ask you some questions about who says what in this clip, whether it's Milosevic or Mikelic. So if you could listen carefully to that and see if you are able to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could play the second clip now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in that clip, one of the two men says, "He said that he made a decision on shelling Zagreb, Karlovac, Sisak. He is a man "what a smart man is ashamed of a crazy man is proud of. He pointed it out as his achievement." Were you able to tell which of the two men said that in the clip?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was listening to the voice and not reading the text. It seems that there has been a mix-up here. Because that was all Milosevic, whereas here it says Mikelic. Perhaps if you want to play the clip again, but I wrote this down as a note to myself because I was listening and I realised this and made a note of what I heard. Milosevic says, well, we heard the statement, we listened to the statement but he said that because of your suffering or something and then he said he made the decision on shelling Zagreb or whatever, Zagreb, Karlovac, Sisak and so on, so I think that I heard that that was all Milosevic speaking, if you want to repeat, then I can make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's play it again to see and it's that second part, that he said he made a decision on shelling Zagreb, Karlovac. I want to you see if you can tell who was saying that second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to tell who says that second part that he said he made a decision on shelling Zagreb, Karlovac, Sisak, he is a man -- "what a smart man is ashamed of a crazy man is part of, he pointed it out as his achievement." Were you able to tell who said that in the clip?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to play another clip which is on page 4 of the English, it's on page 3 of the B/C/S. And this is a clip starts with Milosevic saying, "At the assembly his resignation should be demanded." Do you see where that is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Intercept played].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in that clip, Mr. Milosevic says, "He is a criminal who does not think, he reacts like an animal and not like a man. Yesterday he ordered to shell Zagreb." Who do you understand him to be talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He then makes reference to 7.000 people in encirclement. What do you understand that to be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, yes, about 7.000 civilians and soldiers in an encirclement which were located in the Pakrac area, because the Croatian army and police cut across the escape route to the population and the soldiers towards Banja Luka or the territory of Republika Srpska. They were under siege. They were in an encirclement, the Serbs were encircled by the Croatian police and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did the shelling of Zagreb have any effect on those people who were encircled, in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have led to Croatian retaliation and have the people as victims of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally I want to play a clip -- no, not finally. There are two more. There is -- the fourth clip is on page 5 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. And it starts with Milosevic saying, "It should be said at your assembly."

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In that clip, Milosevic says, "When everything was ready for the motorway to be open, Martic said it was out of question to open the motorway. So after that, Croatia attacked and Tudjman said that he must open the motorway" . What is that a reference to, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that once the motorway was closed off, there were negotiations to reopen it, and it was already agreed that the motorway would be reopened, and then Martic said it was out of the question, and that he would not allow for the motorway to be opened, and this is what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally the last clip, it's on page 6 of the English and it's at the bottom of page 4, top of page 5 of the B/C/S. And it's about halfway down the page on the English, and it starts with Milosevic saying, "He cannot violate the constitution. He caused half of it by violating the constitution." I think it's at the bottom of page 4. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could play that clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in that last clip, Mr. Milosevic says, "He behaves like a mad dog. Even Hitler did not do that. He tore Krajina apart. He is a dangerous troublemaker and a criminal. He is boasting about having shelled Zagreb. The thing a smart man is ashamed of a lunatic is proud of." Who do you understand him to be talking about in that clip?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this intercept be marked for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The intercept 593 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I believe that I have not seen the date of this conversation, and I don't know whether there is an indication to that effect. Could we do that before we mark this document for identification? Otherwise we do not object for this document to be identified, but we would like to have the date in order to avoid any subsequent dispute with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think all I can do now is ask the witness if he has any indication about what the date is based on the context of the statement, and we can put further evidence in about when this intercept was -- what the date of the intercept is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, given the references in the discussion, are you able to tell approximately what the date of the conversation is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been the 3rd or the 4th of May, after the 1st or the 2nd of May so it could have been the 3rd or the 4th of May. At that time, after the shelling of Zagreb, which took place on the 2nd of May. It may have been on the 2nd of May as well, because a mention is made of the second shelling so it could have been on the 2nd but in any case between the 2nd of May and the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There are a number of references to an assembly that is going to occur. Do you recall approximately when that assembly occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a different date, before this conversation took place, and the date is the 17 and 18 of May 1995. So this conversation did take place between the 2nd of May and the 17 of May 1995, and that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Could it be marked for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Intercept 593 is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification number 233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I see the Bench perhaps has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Whiting, I'm very sorry I'm not comprehending. I thought the witness said when you asked him about the date of this assembly that it was a different date before this conversation took place and the date is the 17th and 18th of May 1995. Could we get a clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think -- yes we can try and clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the assembly that's referred to, when did that occur, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th and 18th of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And based on what you have -- what you see in this transcript, are you able to tell whether this conversation occurred before or after the assembly on the 17th and 18th of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I hope that clears it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I asked you with respect to some of the transcripts but I neglected this question with respect to others so I want to put this question to you with respect to all of the intercepts that you've listened to during your testimony and you've spoken about during your testimony here in this trial. And the question is this: With respect to all of the intercepts, are the statements that are made by the people in the conversations consistent with what you understood, what you knew to be their positions at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Having listened to the intercepts and looked at the transcripts and considered them, is there anything that causes you to doubt the authenticity of any of the intercepts that you have spoken about in your testimony here in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, finally, I want to begin -- I want to end where we began. And I want to ask you this. I want you, if you could, to tell the Trial Chamber in your own words what you were responsible for in 1991. What did you plead guilty to? What do you take responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I succumbed to the passions of politics and ethnical egotism. I believed that it would be possible to achieve the goal that Slobodan Milosevic set and that was to create a one-state for all Serbs. I believe that this was doable by ethnic separation without any clashes, starting from an approach within the then political system of Yugoslavia, which said that the municipality is a basic unit and that there is room for self-determination. I used my political authority. I invested it in the organisation of the Serbian Autonomous Province of Krajina. I had my personal fears and I had mistrust of the government of Croatia and I shared those with the people of Krajina and I openly conveyed my fear to these people, and that's how I instigated their mistrust of the government and I also contributed to the hatred between the peoples and the Serbian people towards the Croatian state. I became a popular politician in Krajina. I occupied a highest position in Krajina. I won the trust and I created the institutions of the Serbian Autonomous Province of Krajina. I created its institutions. When the war started and when I realised that the creation of the Greater Serbian state is being carried out by force by the persecution of Croats, I kept quiet and I continued performing my public duties. I did have an opportunity to step back, to resign, to withdraw, but I remained in my position and I became responsible or co-responsible for whatever happened in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to ask just one question, Mr. Babic, on the statement you've just a made. Are you saying that you, Mr. Milan Babic are not responsible for any act of violence against anybody other than for the position you held as Prime Minister of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I'm saying is that I contributed to the acts of violence by performing my duties, by creating institutions, by setting up institutions, one of them being the Territorial Defence, by speaking in public, by instigating people, by persuading them that life in a Serbian state separated from Croats is a guarantee of safety, and I am responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you the same question differently. Have you, during your term as a leader in the SAO Krajina, given an order to anybody to commit crime, to kill anybody, to loot, to destroy homes? You never gave that order to anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Cross-examination, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I am Predrag Milovancevic Defence counsel for Mr. Milan Martic. As for the procedure regulated by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, this is the stage of your cross-examination. Since we speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to make a short pause between my question and your answer so as to help the interpreters to translate our words correctly. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, when you spoke about yourself, you said that you were born in the former Yugoslav Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where you attended primary school, secondary school, when you graduated from the secondary school and when you started studying in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Kukar and I went to primary school in Vrlika which is some three or four kilometres away from my native village and I finished the 8th grade of primary school in Zemun. I graduated from medical school in Belgrade and I graduated in 1974. And then I became a student at the school of dentistry in Belgrade. I completed my studies in 1980 and I graduated one year later. Or actually two years later, to be more precise. During my career in 1988 and 1989, and 1990 as well, I attended post-graduate studies in social medicine at the school of medicine in Sarajevo. I did not obtain my masters degree. I got involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, did I understand you well when you said that in 1982, you became a dentist, you graduated in dentistry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when you started working?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1982, when I became a resident and -- but I interrupted my residency, and I served my compulsory military service and then I started working as a dentist. This was a temporary position but it lasted for a number of years. And then I got a permanent job as a dentist at the medical centre of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about your residency after the compulsory military service, where was that, in which place and what institution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the outpatient's clinic in Djevrske. Also at the outpatient's clinic in Vrlika and the outpatient's clinic in Knin. I passed my board exam at the medical centre of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did you pass your board exam?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the residency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the year, if you remember? This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when you took up your job in Knin at the medical centre of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started my residency there, and I was employed by the medical centre of Knin from September 1982, with some interruptions for the military service, and then I had a temporary position there, but I was continuously at the medical centre of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you become the chief administrator of the medical centre of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became the acting chief administrator after the receivership in 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Amongst your personal data, you also mentioned that you were a member of the League of Communists of Croatia, which means that were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, the interpreter asked that the witness repeat the date. "I became the acting chief administrator after the receivership in 19" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I became the acting chief administrator of the medical centre of Knin in 1989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I've already asked you, Mr. Babic. You said that you were a member of the league of communists of Croatia. When did you become a member?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I did not become a member of the League of Communists of Croatia. I became a member of the League of Communists of Serbia in 1974, while I was still attending high school in Belgrade, and once I moved to Croatia and started working I transferred my documents from the municipal board in Zvezdana to the municipal board in Knin and that's actually how I joined the League of Communists of Croatia and I got involved in its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you became a member of the League of Communists of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Earlier, Mr. Babic said, "I did not become a member of the League of Communists of Croatia. I became a member of the League of Communists of Serbia." Now he says, actually, "how I joined the League of Communists of Croatia and I got involved in its work." Now, did you become a member of the League of Communists of Croatia at some stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I just meant to say the following. This was not my new admission into the League of Communists. The League of Communists of Croatia was part of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. There was just an administrative procedure of transferring my documents from the League of Communists of Serbia to the League of Communists of Croatia, and that's how I became a member of the League of Communists of Croatia. It was not my first admission into the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you ever just mentioned the relationship between the League of Communists of Serbia, the League of Communists of Croatia, and the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Can you please briefly tell us at that time the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was a socialist state, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution, the system was socialist and there was the so-called self-management socialist system. The sociopolitical system was social and self-managing system and I think this is the most precise definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can one say that in Yugoslavia, up to 1990, the ruling party was the League of Communists which was first known as the Communist Party and that it was the only party, the only political organisation. There was also the Socialist Alliance, there was a trade union and other organisations, but this was the only political party. Can you tell us, can you confirm for us that this was a mono-party system?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an integral League of Communists of Yugoslavia which consisted of the League of Communists of the various republics. This was a party organised based on the federal principle within the party itself. The federal relationship between the republican parties within the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Such an organisation of the party, did it enable you to transfer your membership from the League of Communists of Serbia to the League of Communists of Croatia? Actually it was all one and only League of Communists of Yugoslavia, is that what you were saying before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that you formally joined the League of Communists of Croatia as part of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia? Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same year when I started working. It was in 1982, in the autumn of that year, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what positions you held in the party organisation in the League of Communists of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the basic organisation of the League of Communists in the primary health care in Knin up to 1989. In the autumn of that year, I became the secretary of the basic organisation of the League of Communists of the primary health care system in Knin, and I remained in that position until the 17th of February 1990, for a couple of months, that is, during the time surrounding the congress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the League of Communists of Croatia, as well as all the other organisations of communists in other republics, had its organisations at the municipal level, in companies, that the network of party organs was widely spread, and you belonged to the League of Communists in Knin in your workplace?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an alternative for me to either belong to the regional League of Communists or to the company League of Communists. It was customary to belong to the basic organisation that was set up in one's company, and that's how I was a member of the basic organisation in the company that I worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any limitation or difference or any way of differentiating on an ethnic basis the members of the League of Communists of Croatia? What I'm saying is this. In that kind of party organisation, would all people be able to join regardless of a nation -- ethnicity, religion, creed or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You, who were a Serb yourself, your ethnicity was a Serb, and you were employed in Knin, and secretary of the party organisation in your work organisation, you received an invitation to take part at the congress of the League of Communists much Croatia which took place at the end of 1989, am I right when I say that? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to be more specific in my answer. There were a number of points raised there by you. First of all, I was elected as a delegate to the congress. So that's what you meant by your question. Before I was elected secretary of the basic organisation, which means that in the pre-congress preparations that went on during that time. Now, I do apologise but what was your question? What else did you wish to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The explanation is sufficient, Mr. Babic. As a member of the League of Communists of Croatia, under the procedure provided for by the party rules, you were invited to go to the congress and take part in it and you did do so, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't invited to the congress. That's the first point. When it came to that congress, the last congress of the League of Communists of Croatia, in fact, a new procedure was introduced for people going to the congress. Before, the proceedings were that the municipal conference of the League of Communists of the commune would nominate delegates from its community to attend the congress but for the first time, during those elections, it was stated that the delegates to the congress of the League of Communists of Croatia should be elected by a general vote on the part of all the members of the party organisation on the municipality's territory. And for the Knin municipality, there are about 3.700 members of the League of Communists of Croatia, and many in the basic organisations, and I, my name was put forward by my basic organisation to this joint list. My name was placed on the list and it went to all the basic organisations. It was distributed to the general elections, the general party elections that took place at the time and I was elected among the six delegates and that was the way in which I was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So as one of six delegates, who represented those 3.700 members of the League of Communists in Knin, you went to attend the party congress and where was the venue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Zagreb, at the fair grounds, the Velesajam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen at the congress that would be of specific importance to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two important things happened. The first was this: The decision by the congress to introduce a multi-party system into the political system of Croatia. The second decision was a decision which delved into statutory measures of the organisation of the League of Communists of Croatia and Yugoslavia and it was the following. It was decided at the congress that the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was a collection of the leagues of communists of the republics or rather it was defined in this way, that the League of Communists of Croatia was not a part of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia but that the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was composed of the League of Communists organizations in the republics and provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This decision immediate by the League of Communists of Croatia at their congress, did it mean the break-up of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia as a united organization and ensuring complete independence for the League of Communists of Croatia? Is that what that meant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes. Not the break-up but new relationships within the League of Communists of Yugoslavia which became a federation of the party organisations of the republics, and the Serb members, the Serb delegates to the congress also voted on that. I think that there were 25 per cent Serbs taking part at the congress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in favour of the decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I belonged to the minority who voted for a united league of communists of Yugoslavia as one organisation and we were not in favour of changing the Statute, the statutory decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the congress of the League of Communists of Croatia, in view of the fact that the League of Communists of Yugoslavia had its own statute, did the congress of the League of Communists of Croatia, was it in your opinion the right decision to adopt, viewed at from the aspects of the statute of the party of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and from the party statute aspect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert in statutory matters but as I understood it, the decision was statutory, although I didn't agree with it. But as I say, I can't give you an exact answer to that question, and interpret the statute. All I can tell you is how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the reasons for which you opposed the decision to which the League of Communists much Croatia would become independent and as such represent a part of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw in that step a sort of domination by the nationalist element and a form of a nationalist approach, an ethnic approach, within the League of Communists of Croatia. So how shall I put this, a sort of ethno-philotism in the party organisation of Croatia, and in view of the fact that the party was still in power, this certainly had to have its consequences or repercussions on the functioning of the federation or rather the socialist federal republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what could those repercussions have been on the federation. How could this have influenced the functioning of the federation, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that for a long time, among Croatian public opinion but we are now talking about the League of Communists of Croatia, from 1971 onwards, there was a dominant national or ethnic stream which went towards a confederalisation of relations within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, there was a stream which interpreted the constitution of Yugoslavia in a special way because it said in the constitution of Yugoslavia that the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was composed of the republics, made up of six republics and the people, the nations, and then these were stipulated, all the nations which made up the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the Slovenes, the Croats, the Muslims, the Serbs, the Montenegrins, the Macedonians. Have I omitted someone? Anyway, I'm talking about this stream or faction that existed in the League of Communists of Croatia which interpreted this and explained the constitution, interpreted it, as stating that this unification of the republics and unity of the republics of the nations and nationalities into a Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had not been exhausted ones and for all but that the republics or rather the people, the nations, had the right to open up the question again at a certain point in time, which was a different interpretation to the dominant, prevailing position, and the politics waged at that time within the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and generally in the other republics, that the right to create a federation and to unite within a country called Yugoslavia had been exhausted, that you can't reassess it, re-evaluate it. I think I've made myself clear it enough. If not, I can go on to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. You have explained that to us in great detail. Now, this kind of nationalist stream within the League of Communists of Croatia and you said that it existed from 1971, tried to do something on the political arena in Yugoslavia itself, in that in 1971, the maspok, maspok which was the mass movement. What did that mean, mass movement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That stream was defeated in 1971 by the intervention made by Josip Broz Tito at the time and in Croatia from 1971, to 1979, or rather until the end of 1989 there was a more moderate stream which at that last congress in 1989 started to open up the whole question and broach the whole question of -- that was raised in 1971 but not in such an extremist, nationalistic way that was done in what was known as the maspok in 1971, the mass movement, and, of course, you know what the maspok referred to and signified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since we mentioned this mass movement or maspok, as it was called, can you tell us very briefly what it actually means so as to clarify this issue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the politics waged by the then leadership of the League of Communists of Croatia led by Savka Dabcevic Kucar, Miko Tripalo, and they gained broad support by the different nationalist organisations of Croatia for a confederalisation of Yugoslavia, and to all intents and purposes, it called for Croatia's independence by the same token, and which this would end up by having Croatia move for membership in the United Nations. So that was the level it went up to and the level of changes in relationships in Yugoslavia that it called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if I've understood you correctly in that year of 1971, the leadership of Croatia called for an independent Croatia and its reception into the United Nations as a member?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this demand was overturned by Josip Broz Tito. Was he the president of Yugoslavia and the president of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what ethnicity Josip Broz Tito was himself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody knew that he was a Croat, although in the Belgrade press, lots of things were written about all this but we all believed that he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us how it was that Josip Broz Tito vanquished that stream, the 1971 stream, that called for Croatia's independence and its becoming a member of the United Nations in that year of 1971?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He held a session in Karadjordjevo, a meeting in Karadjordjevo with the political leadership of the day. I can't remember all the people that were there. Well, he replaced the leadership, in fact, the political leadership in Croatia, and while he was at it, a large-scale manoeuvres were taking place by the army on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, those manoeuvres, were they entitled Freedom 71? Was that the name given to the manoeuvres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this demand for breaking up Yugoslavia and Croatia's secession in 1971 ended by the replacement of the Croatian leadership and in 1974 the new constitution of Yugoslavia was adopted; is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the proviso that in the meantime constitutional amendments were adopted to the constitution of Yugoslavia between 1971 and 1974, I mean, so that the 1974 constitution just incorporated the amendments that had already been adopted and gave definitive shape and introduced new relationships between the republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in such a way as that although the country was a federation in name, it actually became a confederation in essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this would be a good opportunity to take our break, if that is agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take our break and come back at quarter to 11. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry about that little delay. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we left off mentioning the new constitution of Yugoslavia or rather the then constitution of Yugoslavia dating back to 1974, and you said of that constitution that, in fact, it turned Yugoslavia into a confederation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia pursuant to the constitution was still a federation but the structure relationship between republics and provinces by the new -- under the new 1974 constitution was changed. Or rather we can say that the Croatian movement in 1971 was defeated but that the demands of that movement were incorporated into the constitution, and Yugoslavia did indeed become a confederation, by virtue of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was personally the Croatian leadership, the political leadership of 1971, that the political leadership was defeated because Josip Broz Tito replaced them as president of Yugoslavia, I mean Josip Broz Tito. Now, can you give us some well known names from that 1971 year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned them. Two political leaders, one was the secretary or rather the party head of the League of Communists of Croatia Savka Dabcevic Kucar, and the second name was Miko Tripalo. There were more but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. What about Pero Pirker, was he among them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Ivan Zvonimir Cicak, although he wasn't in the party, Drazan Budisa?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cicak and Budisa were students at the time. They were not in the party or rather one of them, whether he studied theology, I think, I'm not quite sure, but I don't think they were members of the party. Budisa and Cicak but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The movement for Croatia's independence in 1971, that you talked about, did it include just the party functionaries or were there other members as well? Do you know anything about the fate of Janko Bobetko, Stjepan Mesic, Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maspok was in fact a concept for a broader social movement going on in Croatia at the time. The League of Communists of Croatia -- well, I can't tell you specifically about the relationships within the movement but the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was part of that movement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, League of Communists of Croatia, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I said that different organisations such as the Matica Hrvatska, with Croatian attributes was part of it and they were leaders of the maspok in the society of Croatia, so Matica Hrvatska, was the most extreme or extremist organisation within the frameworks of that movement and the movement itself is linked to Matica Hrvatska. And now all the people, the names, I can't remember them all from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. In the 1970s, and later on, the president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, was he convicted for Croatian nationalism and was he sentenced to a term in prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that when Tudjman was head of the HDZ and a presidential candidate or rather when he had already become president of Croatia. I heard information about that from a man who had taken part in Tudjman's trial. But from that time, from 1971, I really don't know firsthand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the trial took place? Are you talking about the 1970s now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking about that time but as I say I heard about it in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to hear that the present president of the Republic of Croatia, Stjepan Mesic, as president of the Orahovac municipality was given a prison term for Croatian nationalism during those 1970s?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what his position was but I knew -- do know that he spent time in prison in Stara Gradiska for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that General Janko Bobetko, the Chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army, in the 91 to 95 events, was pensioned off in 1971 and he also had problems because of Croatian nationalism?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since we have been using the term maspok, is that in fact an abbreviation of two words, mass movement, and whether for that mass movement, the other name was the Croatian Spring and we are talking about 1971?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Babic, anything about an event on Mount Radusa near Bugojno in Bosnia-Herzegovina that took place in 1972?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what I heard from the mass media, from the press, and what happened in my surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that year, as far as we were informed by the press, a group of Croatian emigres, as they were referred to -- they were referred to as Ustashas, they illegally crossed into some cistern or some kind of truck, they managed to come in from abroad, on a vehicle, into Yugoslavia, and they got out at mount Radusa in western Hercegovina which is between Bosnia and Herzegovina. Their objective was to raise an armed uprising a rebellion, and -- against Yugoslavia, and as I myself was in my native village at that time, during that summer, I know that there was movement on the part of the police, that the group was -- they went out to apprehend the group. I think that many of them were taken prisoner and liquidated and that was the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be wrong if I say that of the 19 members of that group in that operation, 18 were liquidated and that the army and police forces in Yugoslavia or rather that the police and army forces of Yugoslavia had a number of casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge, 18 to 19 casualties in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the killing of Ambassador Rolovic in Stockholm, the capital of Sweden. He was the ambassador of Yugoslavia to Sweden and his killing in 1971 and who did the killing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. I was at school in Zvezdana and our school was tasked with carrying flowers when Ambassador Rolovic was being buried in the new cemetery in Belgrade. And this had been done by a member of the Sosi [phoen] immigration as we were told. I forget his name. He was arrested and he was arrested, he was imprisoned in Sweden, but the name may still come to me. But I'll tell you later if it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The two assassins, were they Miro Barisic and Ajdjelko Brajkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember Barisic but I can't remember the other name, doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did they storm into the embassy of Yugoslavia in the capital of Sweden and they killed the ambassador by shooting in -- a bullet in his mouth? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the event was described in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this Ustasha terrorist, Miro Barisic, after his escape, went to Paraguay and instructed special units in martial arts, and then in 1991 he joined the Croatian police and he was killed by the Serbian peasants at the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he escaped from Sweden, I don't know where he found himself. I know that he was killed in 1991, somewhere on the line separating the Krajina Police and the Croatian police. I heard that, and even here in this happening, imprisoned people asked me if I knew who was it who had killed this Barisic. I don't know who it was and this would be the answer to your question, actually to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was it who asked you in the detention unit about the killers of Barisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladen Naletilic, Tuta. Tuta asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that person is and how come he's here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in the detention unit here. He is a Croat from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: He is accused by the Tribunal. Are you referring to that person? That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The late Miro Barisic, the assassin, the killer of an ambassador of Yugoslavia, did he die as a member of the Croatian police, the police of Franjo Tudjman, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was he on the Serbian side or on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that he was on the Croatian side but I don't know anything about the event itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, was it in that context that you used the term Ustasha terrorist of Miro before in your previous question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After the reminiscing on 1991 I have another question, Mr. Babic. Do you remember or do you know anything about a similar movement for Slovenian independence in Slovenia before the year 1971? Do you know anything about the road scandal? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't have enough information as to be able to say anything about that. I don't know what happened before 1971 in Croatia -- in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the top leadership in Croatia that wanted Croatia to be admitted into the United Nations in 1971, were eventually replaced by Josip Broz Tito?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Savka Dabcevic Kucar and Miko Tripalo were removed from their offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have also told us that despite the defeat of the top leadership in Croatia, there were some changes to the constitution in 1974 which meant essential changes of the state of Yugoslavia, which was still a federation but was gradually turning into a confederation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be wrong or let me put it in another way: The main authors of the 1974 constitution, were they Slovenian Edvard Kardelj and a Croat, Vladimir Bakaric, and together with them Josip Broz Tito, the Croat who adopted all that as the president of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But also the political leaderships of Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, Macedonia, of all the republics, in other words. Otherwise, there could not have been any amendments to the constitution, if there was no consensus on the part of everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that after all of these events that we have just talked about, towards the end of 1989, you participated in the party congress of the League of Communists of Croatia and that one could hear new theories about the position of that party. Were they similar to the theories that were heard in 1971 or did you perceive them as such?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I felt a certain level of ethno-philotism, and that's putting it mildly. Not in the League of Communists of Croatia and not in the way as it was in 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, in 1989, when this congress of the League of Communists of Croatia took place, already from February 1989, there was the Croatian Democratic Union in place as a party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the Croatian democratic union was established. I don't know exactly, but what I know is that after the congress and the changes to the legislation of Croatia, at the beginning of 1990, it was one of the first parties that had been set up as part of the pluralist political system of Croatia that was set up after the congress of the League of Communists of Croatia. I don't know when this happened, whether it was in February or in some other time. I don't know when the HDZ was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tudjman participated in the meeting on the 24th and 25th of February 1990, in the founding meeting of the HDZ, and he said that this organisation had been active as of February 1989, and when this congress took place, it became a political organisation and it was registered as such. Was it registered even before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been registered before the congress because it took the changes to the legislation in order to register new parties. So the parliament had to pass new laws in order for any new parties to be registered. Is that the answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Can you tell us when the law was passed that allowed multi-party organisation of the political life in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either in late 1989 or early 1990, the beginning of 1990 it was already in force and the date for a multi-party election was set. I believe that it happened already at the congress of the League of Communists of Croatia before the procedure itself to adopt legal norms was passed or the date and the time of the first multi-party elections in Croatia was already set and I remember that there was a lot of debate about that, whether this was premature or not, and I know that the -- either the president or the secretary of the party organization of Zagreb, whatever his title was, opposed to such an early setup of the date of the elections. He was of the opinion that this was premature. I remember those details very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, a law was passed that provided the grounds for the multi-party system in Croatia and a number of new parties appeared on the political scene of Croatia. Do you remember any of them? Can you tell us their names and who their leaders were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the congress and after the laws were passed, until the elections which were held in April and May, the League of Communists of Croatia was gradually transformed and it changed the name. It was changed into SDP which was the party of democratic changes. Then the Croatian Democratic Union was established or rather registered as such. Then there was the Croatian Democratic Party, the Serbian Democratic Party, the Yugoslav independent democratic party, I'm not sure whether the Socialist Party of Croatia was established before or after the elections. Its head was Boro Mikelic, and there was also the Socialist Party of Croats or the Socialist Alliance of the working people of Croatia which was transformed into a new party under the name of the Socialist Party of Croatia and this also happened before the elections. I don't know whether there were any other parties. There must have been but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It's enough, Mr. Babic. We mentioned some political figures from the political life of Croatia that were active in 1971, Savka Dabcevic and Miko Tripalo namely, and we also mentioned Mr. Tudjman. In 1990, did Savka Dabcevic took the leadership of a new party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me try and remember its name. I can't give you its precise name. I don't know whether she was with the two Veselica brothers in the Croatian people's party or whether she founded her own party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Tripalo, was he a member of a new party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with Savka. He was a member of her party. They were members of the same party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Budisa, did he establish a party or did he belong to a party, Drazen Budisa?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember the name of his party. I don't know whether they immediately registered themselves as the Croatian Liberal Party or something similar to that. I don't know. Maybe they were called the Liberal Democratic Party. In any case, that was their name later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It is a notorious fact that Mr. Franjo Tudjman became the first president of the Croatian Democratic Union and there is no dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stipan Mesic was also, a high-ranking policemen of that party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the HDZ. He was just a politician in that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the HDZ, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say in very general terms that all the people who had problems on account of the Croatian nationalism in 1971 and were removed from politics, all of a sudden in 1990 appeared on the scene as the leaders of the best-known new parties in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I knew about these people in 1971, they re-appeared in 1990, all of them save for Cicak who was probably a member of a non-party organisation, of a non-governmental organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we were talking about this Croatian Spring as it was known or the maspok that took place in 1971. In 1971, did that political option have an impact on the Croatian population or the population of Croatia? How did people perceive that? How did you perceive 1971?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year 1971 caused a lot of ethnic tensions and some political regrouping. I've already mentioned the fact that Croatian nationalists and advocates of the independent state of Croatia rallied around Matica Hrvatska and on the other hand, the Serbs rallied around Prosvjeta. Both these institutions were, on the paper, cultural and arts societies but at that time they became the fosterers of political ideas. As a consequence there was a lot of mistrust, a raised level of fear among the Serbs, especially after the year 1972 and the infiltration of the terrorist group that we mentioned and also the idea of an independent state of Croatia which started being prominent in the Croatian society and in the Croatian general public also gave rise to fear and these are the consequences that lingered on in society.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned certain fear in 1971 and 1972. Who was afraid? What were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the fear that existed amongst the Serbs because I could notice that in the area where I was, in 1971, the Serbs were afraid, they didn't know what the number of the -- and the strength of that group of immigrants was, the group that was infiltrated. The Serbs feared for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, that political option, the option of independence, and leaving the Yugoslav federation and asking for membership in the United Nations, did this also cause fear amongst the Serb population? Were there any reactions to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to define a fear but I can say that there was a counter-political movement which had its origin in the cultural, Serbian cultural society called Prosvjeta. This was a reaction to -- and there was an escalation of political positions that were based on ethnicity and I think that this would be the best description of the relationship that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that congress of the League of Communists of Croatia in 1989, where did you vote against the decision for the League of Communists of Croatia to become independent and you were among a very few who voted against that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were two decisions on the table. I voted for the multi-party system but I was against the second decision because I believed the League of Communists had prevalence in society and that it was still ruling -- the ruling party and that it will remain the ruling party even after the multi-party elections, for -- at least for some time, and that there was an imminent danger that a new political option would lead to separation and break-up of republics in Yugoslavia. This was my line of thought at the time, and this is the reason why I voted for the former constitutional and statutory decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that towards the end of 1989, the new law on multi-party organisation of the state was passed and that the new multi-party -- and that the first multi-party elections were called for the month of April 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what were the political situation was at the time? What was the political campaign in the run-up to the first multi-party elections especially in view of the Croatian population -- of the Serbian population of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The campaign in Croatia started in 1989 and intensified. The main issue on the agenda was something that was outside of Croatia, namely the incidents in Kosovo and the celebration of the 600th anniversary of the Kosovo battle, and this was used to polarise society in Croatia. The first movement was among -- in the trade union of Croatia which supported miners in Trepca whereas Serb members of the trade union in some companies advocated the political option introduced by Serbia in Kosovo. Already in 1989, this became a topical issue and at the beginning of 1990 and in the run-up to the multi-party elections, were still among the most topical issues. And then, of course, the political parties that were set up in early 1990 and appeared in the political campaign and on the political scene in the run-up to the second round of elections in May 1990, they advocated political changes; there was a competition of political ideas amongst these parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These events in Kosovo and as you said the support of the Croatian trade unions to the Albanian claims in Kosovo, did that start in 1989 or did it actually start earlier? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when was it that they started exactly? But things escalated in 1980, I think, in February, when the trade union supported the miners in the Trepca mines who were on strike. So it was the trade unions of Croatia that supported them. Whereas the Serbs supported the intervention or the political leadership of Serbia towards the miners and towards Kosovo. That is when big rallies were held, rallies of support, to this policy in Knin, Lapac, et cetera, whereas at the same time the federation of the trade unions of Croatia and Slovenia, I think, were collecting aid for the strikers in the Trepca mine. So I remember that, and I remember that this polarisation actually came to the fore then, and these political clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These miners in Trepca, Mr. Babic, were they of Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were they on strike because they sought better working conditions or did they have some other demands?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was in the context of political demands in Kosovo that were there for many years, and at that time, they escalated. I cannot give you the exact time but there were demonstrations by students, the general population, workers, in favour of proclaiming Kosovo a republic. There was an intervention by the federal authorities, a federal detachment of the police was set up there. I know that because some policemen from Croatia also went to this detachment which controlled the situation there. I cannot give you the exact time-frame when all of this happened. I simply heard about it from the media. I was following it from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, I just wonder if we could get a clarification on the time, the year, here. Because in answer to a previous question, it's at line 19, there may have been a misinterpretation but it says 1980 whereas in previous answers it was I believe 1990. So perhaps this could be clarified what year approximately we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to do that for us, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we are at it I was about to ask whether are we likely to come to the relevant period to the case? We've been dealing with history from 1971 and it looks like we are outside the period of the indictment. I'm not quite sure when you hope to get there, if you can give us an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I actually wanted to get to this answer through the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But let's clarify there particular matter, Mr. Babic. These protests of Albanian miners in Trepca, when did they actually take place? The transcript does not reflect the exact year, 88, 80, when was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was during the course of 1988 until the beginning of February 1989. I cannot say exactly. I just know that in February 1989, there was an escalation of different reactions in society on account of these events. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to put one more question to you in relation to this particular topic, very briefly. You said that at that time, Albanians in Kosovo were asking for a republic, the federal authorities intervened, and you also said that Slovenia and Croatia support this demand for independence. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that the Croatian and Slovenian trade unions were collecting aid contributions for the miners who were in the Trepca mines on strike. This was a drive by the trade unions of Croatia and then the trade union of a factory in Knin reacted and they condemned the Croatian trade unions for supporting the miners. That's February 1989. And there was a social confrontation in Croatia on account of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since these are political events that do not have to do with this case, really, but just a brief question. What about the demands of the Trepca miners who were sitting in the mines? Were they -- were their demands political or did they want to have better working conditions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. While answering the questions of the Prosecutor and also in your statements, you said that after this congress of the League of Communists of Croatia in 1989, that you participated in, at the beginning of 1990 you heard of the Serb Democratic Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On TV Belgrade, I think that it was on the day of St. Sava, the 27th of January, I saw academician Raskovic making a statement, after a rally in Donji Lapac; he announced that a Serb party would be established. He didn't say what its actual name would be but he said that it would be a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the establishment of this kind of party announced by Mr. Raskovic at a moment when there was already a law that made it possible to establish different political parties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This Serb Democratic Party that was established in the territory of the then Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, was it registered according to Croatian laws and the federal law?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, first it was registered according to the Croatian law and a few months later it was also registered at the federal Secretariat for Justice that dealt with this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
