utterances.text: Does that mean that a decision was passed by a relevant authority of the Republic of Croatia, the ministry for justice and administration, that's probably what it was called, and in this way, was the Serb Democratic Party registered in accordance with the programme that contained its political goals?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was registered, this party was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to this decision, could the Serb Democratic Party operate in the territory of all of Croatia and could it operate in the territory of Yugoslavia as such?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This possibility of political activity on the part of the Serb Democratic Party stemmed on the one hand from the decision of the relevant Croatian authorities that it could function in the territory of Croatia and also at the same time it was registered at federal level by the appropriate authorities in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't at the same time. It was a bit later, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said at the same time in a figurative sense. I hope that we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see this document on the registration of the Serb Democratic Party, this document of the Ministry of Justice and Administration of the Republic of Croatia, and what does it say in it? What are the objectives of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in general terms what it says in this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that decision, there are two or three sentences in terms of what the programme of the party is. Briefly, well, now, I would have to repeat it, but perhaps I can just tell you about it in my own words. After all, I handed in a document, and it exists there, and that is where it is precisely specified what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say in this document that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I'm wondering if the -- if Mr. Milovancevic is going to put a document to the witness, whether it could be shown to the witness, for him to comment on it, if that's what's intended here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Will you show the witness the document you want to talk about? And possibly also show it to your learned friend on the opposite side and to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is possible. I proceeded from the statement that the witness gave on the 31st of January 2006, wherein the tabs on page 2 of that statement, in tab 2, there is a brief account of the text of that decision, so I thought that the presentation of the document in its entirety would just be time-consuming. That's why I didn't want to produce the document itself. I believe that there is nothing controversial about it. The witness should know what he said in his statement and what the content of this document is. I don't think it is necessary for us to dwell on it now, to find the document. Of course, if you consider this to be necessary I shall do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you can do so without looking at a document yourself. But once you start picking up the document and you want the witness to comment on the content of the document, then we've got to know whether you intend to tender that document into evidence, you've got to show it to the witness, and show it to the rest of the people who participate in the proceedings. If, however, that's -- you don't intend tendering it into evidence, you can ask the question and let's see whether the witness can remember what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Babic, what it said in principle, this decision about the objectives of the political party and why its registration was allowed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party shall advocate the introduction of a multi-party system, of a free market in society, also the freedom of speech, of assembly, rule of law, then federal relations within Yugoslavia, regionalisation. Now, what it says exactly in the decision is probably a shorter form. Now, I don't know whether it was all enumerated in the decision itself but these are the basic programme tenets of the party, as was stated in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation, Mr. Babic. This is Exhibit 138, which is part of the evidence, so I believe that there is no need to produce this yet again. As far as I can remember, I think that you quoted it correctly. However, what I would like to ask you is the following: You participated in the founding meetings of that party.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained the reasons for your attendance at these meetings, and your becoming a high official of that party. Can you tell us what these questions were that were of such vital importance for the Serbs living in Croatia? What did the party deal with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned three main questions and reasons. That is the democratisation of the society itself recognition, that is to say introducing a pluralist multi-party system, introducing a free market, the rule of law, and legality, and so on and so forth. All of that is part of the democratisation of society and doing away with the communist legacy. Another question was the protection of Serb national interests in Croatia, and thirdly the third question was regionalisation, that the party advocated. Since I belonged to a region where Serbs were the predominant population, the programme of the party met my political positions and my assessment that the party would be successful with this kind of programme in the region of Knin where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. For those reasons, you became a member of that party, and then, due to various circumstances and developments, you became one of its officials, too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before that you were a member of the League of Communists of Croatia. Can you tell us whether, in the League of Communists of Croatia and the moment when you enter this new political party, did you personally ever display any nationalist positions or any kind of hatred? Did you have any feelings of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This programme of the party that was verified by a republican authority that registered the party, did it contain anything that seemed extremist, nationalist, impermissible, non-democratic to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that one of the questions that this party was supposed to deal with was the question of the Serb people in Croatia. Can you tell us briefly, the then Republic of Croatia as a member of the Yugoslav federation, what was the population of Croatia then and what percentage were Serbs, the Serb people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last census dated back to 1981 so I'm going to give approximate figures now. Croatia had about 4 and a half million inhabitants, perhaps a bit more. Out of that, there were about 12 per cent Serbs or a bit more than that. There were a few percentage points of Yugoslavs and others, other nations and nationalities, as it was called at the time, if you meant the ethnic composition of the population of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I meant, Mr. Babic. So in the structure of the population of the Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, Serbs comprised 12 per cent or, can you remember the actual numbers, the actual figures? I'm not insisting, I'm not insisting that you remember all figures in detail but roughly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were about 530.000 of them, a bit over 500.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and we've already spoken about this, where it was that the Serbs of Croatia lived, in terms of territory and then we'll come to the towns later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before he answers that question, can I clarify one point? Earlier at line 13, the answer starting at line 13, Mr. Babic said that Serbs constituted about 12 per cent or a little bit more than that, of the population. And then there were a few percentage points of Yugoslavs. Now, are Yugoslavs an ethnic group or is the term Yugoslav, does it describe the entire population? Because you then say Yugoslavs and others, other nations and nationalities, as it was called at the time. If you meant the ethnic composition of the population of Croatia. Can you clear that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According to the rules on stating your ethnicity, and right to state your ethnicity during a population census, there were categories as to how people could declare themselves, ethnically speaking. So there were -- was a list of nations and nationalities under certain numbers, for statistical processing, and when the census was taken you could declare yourself in different ways. You could declare yourself as being a Croat, a Serb, a Slovene, et cetera. Those were the nations or the nationalities or ethnic groups which were Italians, for example, Hungarians, Albanians, and so forth. So those are the nations and nationalities. Then you could not declare yourself in any one of those ways, and then there was a separate category. People who did not declare themselves on an ethnic basis and then there was the category of those who would -- could declare themselves on a regional basis as being a Dalmatian, a Bosnian, and so on and so forth, without it being a national category, a Slavonian or whatever. And then there was ha this additional category of Yugoslav. You could declare yourself a Yugoslav. And that was always the very interesting question of what this is. Was this a national affiliation or was it a regional affiliation, or what was it? So I couldn't give you a clear-cut definition but it is closer to the national option rather than regional. So according to some assessments, these were people from mixed marriages, for example, the children of a mixed marriage or people who did not wish -- who were one nationality but didn't want to stress their national or ethnic affiliation and perhaps declared themselves in the political sense as being Yugoslavs. Either to cover up their nationality or to highlight the Yugoslav nation as being a nationality, your nationality. I apologise if I've taken up too much of the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. The other question that came from Mr. Milovancevic was where did the Serbs of Croatia live in Croatia, in terms of territory, in case you had forgotten that, Mr. Milovancevic, that was your question, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you wish me to comment, taking the regions and the municipalities or broader regions? Or generally, do you wish my answer to be a general one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, let's just avoid interrupting each other or overlapping for the benefit of the interpreters, otherwise they are going to have problems, but just one question. The constitution of Yugoslavia according to that constitution, the members of all the nationalities or ethnic groups living on the territory of Yugoslavia were divided into nations and national minorities. Now, the name for these national minorities that was used -- or was the term national minority used in a different sense? You mentioned, you touched upon that issue a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the population was divided into members of nations and they were the majority nations in Yugoslavia and the nationalities which in fact represented the national minorities and the members of ethnic groups that did not belong to either category, either to the nations or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. That will suffice. I asked you the question so that the Trial Chamber could understand a specific feature of the Yugoslav constitution, and that is this: Who were the nations in Yugoslavia, Narodi?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the constitution the nations of Yugoslavia was the she convenience, the Croats, the Muslims, the Serbs, the Montenegrins, and the Macedonians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All the others, all the rest, were called or referred to as nationalities which was a synonym for a national minority, can we state it in those terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not everybody came under the national minority category. They were national minorities or ethnic groups that came under the term nationality, narodnosti.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two categories, in fact. The nationalities and the ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the constitution, did we have the Yugoslav nations, thew Serb nation, the Croat nation, the Slovenian nation, were the Yugoslavs a nation or not pursuant to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when Her Honour asked me, I tried to explain what the concept of Yugoslav, a Yugoslav consisted of. Do you want me to repeat what I said because that's what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will be enough, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We were discussing the issue of the areas in Croatia inhabited by Serbs, what those were. But before we go into that, one more question. Pursuant to the constitution, were the Serbs a nation until 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the sense of constitutional establishment that the state was a state of the Croatian people or Croatian nation, and a state of the Serb people in Croatia. That was the constitutional category.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just one slight intervention. In line 14, it says, were the Serbs a nation until 1992, it wasn't 1992. It was 1990. 1990 was the date when the Croatian constitution underwent amendments. Thank you. I just wanted to take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So the Serbs lived in Croatia as they -- it being their own republic and they had the position of a nation just as the Croats had, the Croats were a nation and the Serbs were a nation under the Croatian constitution; is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what areas, not the municipalities, just the general areas, regions, inhabited by Serbs within the Republic of Croatia, where they lived as a nation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs lived throughout the republic, the Socialist Republic of Croatia as a nation but they were the majority population in Northern Dalmatia, eastern Lika, Kordun, Banija, those areas, and part of Western Slavonia, whereas in other areas, for example, they represented -- well, they also represented a significant portion of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the Serbs in Croatia in 1990, did they live in Croatian towns as well, towns throughout Croatia, the urban population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Zagreb there were 6 per cent, for example, in Rijeka, Split, Dubrovnik. That sort of percentage, 5 or 6 per cent. Yes, they lived in the big towns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, please, Mr. Milovancevic, before you proceed, I'd like to know this from the witness. Did not the persons within the different republics, the six, for example, the Croatians, Macedonians, Slovenians, et cetera, did they not have a sense of identity based on the fact that they were Yugoslavian in a federation that was Yugoslavia? There was not that concept at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That Yugoslav identity was not a national or ethnic identity. It was a political identity, as the citizens of a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It was not a reality in terms of how they perceived themselves as part of their identity, you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not their national identity. Yugoslav-hood was not a national identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But there was no separate group that would be known as Yugoslavs, it was a composite description for persons not clearly fit into the other groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I see you're having difficulty after the description is in. I don't know if I'm the only one in the Chamber or in the courtroom that is having a difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two categories in which one could declare oneself as being a Yugoslav. A Yugoslav in the sense of national affiliation or something similar to that, in Yugoslavia, based on the census. This represented 4, 5, 6 per cent of the population, that category. The category of people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs. And that would be something similar to national affiliation. So in Croatia, which is what I was talking about, 6 or -- roughly 6 or 7 per cent of the population according to the population census declared themselves as being Yugoslavs. That is to say something that could be termed a national category. But it was not -- they were not recognised as a nation or nationality on the basis of the constitution, either of Yugoslavia or the republics. If I might try and explain this a little better, there was a lack of national declaration. If somebody declared themselves as being Yugoslav, they did not wish to declare themselves as being a member of one of the six nations. That would be closest to an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we were discussing the 1974 constitution, and you said that the confederal element came to expression there. Now, what the Trial Chamber is in fact asking you now, it is even difficult for us who lived in that country to understand something like that because in America, an American is an American, whereas in Yugoslavia, you could be a Serb or a Croat or a Macedonian or a Muslim or a Montenegrin but all you couldn't be pursuant to the constitution was a Yugoslav because a Yugoslav was not a nation. Would that help you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thank you. What I know from the scientific terms used or scholarly terms used in the world, there are two types of nation. One is the American type or perhaps the French type in Europe, where citizenship is synonymous with nation and there is the European type of nation, for instance in Europe, where you have Italians, Serbs, Croats and so on which is somewhat different a somewhat different concept to the American concept of nation. So that's the best I can do on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have one more minute, Your Honour. Perhaps we could round off that topic in that minute. My last question in that area, when it comes to a population census, the inhabitants in each of the Yugoslav republics and in the then Yugoslavia had the possibility of declaring themselves as to what nation they belonged to, whether they were Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Macedonians, and all the rest, don't have to go into enumerating them all, but they also had the option of not declaring themselves in that way but stating that we are Yugoslavs. So are those the Yugoslavs you had in mind when you spoke about that category of the population census at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it would be of any use to go on discussing that topic and it's time for the break as well, Your Honours, so if that is agreeable, perhaps we should take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more with you. Court adjourned, to come back at half past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Babic, we looked at the national composition of the Republic of Croatia, the Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, in that year of 1990. And we heard from you that after the congress of the League of Communists of Croatia that was held in 1989 or the end of 1989, that you joined the Serbian Democratic Party. Can you tell us the political reason you chose to take that step and leave the League of Communists of Croatia to join the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already said something about that. First of all, the party programme was in favour of the democratisation of society which meant leaving behind the communist past and introducing a multi-party pluralist system of free market relations and so on and so forth, not to enumerate all the aspect. The second reason was because the party in its programme envisaged the protection of the Serbs in Croatia, who represented the majority in the area of Knin. And that was my third reason, in fact, my desire to give my contribution to the region's development. So in view of the fact that the party had that kind of programme, political programme, and I thought that they would gain support in my region I close to join it. So those were the three reasons for my doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us I think that the League of Communists of Croatia and you attended its last congress in December 1989, made the decision to introduce a multi-party system and to call multi-party elections and schedule them, and could you not wage that struggle for democratisation within the League of Communists of Croatia, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already stated my reasons for joining the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The League of Communists of Croatia, which changed its name into the Party of Democratic Change at the time, so that was the new name, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia Party of Democratic Change, did that party take into account Serb interests in Croatia, the interests of the Serb people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that party, or rather we had the party standing behind everything, as it was called at the time, the previous year and in the bygone period before the multi-party elections were conducted introduced certain changes and in the name given to the language which shook the Serb population. So that was one reason for which I called those tendencies within that party ethno-philotism, ethno-phile or pro-Croatian orientation of a bourgeois nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that that party in that year, were you thinking of 1989, decided to change, make linguistic changes? How can it do so and what was the substance of those changes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said the party stood behind all this because it was in power. It was in power in the Sabor or Croatian assembly. I've already spoken about that. The Croatian assembly, parliament, passed changes in the language, and in the terms, and the party was behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Sabor of Croatia was the Croatian assembly, in other words; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the Serb equivalent or the eastern expression of Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian, as the language was once called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what were the changes in language? What kind of changes were these? Do you know that in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the name of the language itself recognition as I've already said, the language used to be called Croato-Serbian in official use it was Croato-Serbian in Croatia, that was the official name by which the language went. Now, the change in name, the first change in name, took place during the power of the League of Communists of Croatia in 1989, because there were changes during the HDZ in the 1990s, in the 1990s. So this first change was the change in the name of the language itself, and we had a rather unusual construction for the language's name, and then it was said that in official use in Croatia, the Croatian literary language, which is called either the Croatian language or the Serb language, would be in use. That was the formulation with respect to the name of the language, and it represented a Croatisation or the concept of a common language for both Serbs and Croats but it still somehow satisfied form because they sort of said, well, it's the same thing, if somebody says the Serb language, that would mean the Croatian language as well or if somebody spoke about this Croatian language that would imply the Serb language as well. Now, Croatian literary language, that was a question that needed to be debated, what did that mean in political terms and other terms, and that was the situation before the multi-party elections took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this question of language, was it a linguistic issue, first and foremost or a political issue, first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was primarily a political issue and then a linguistic issue because with the language having its name, you had subsequent changes in lexicology and the introduction of dialects, for instance, dialect concepts, from Croatian and archaic terms of the old Croatian language. Well, I'm not a linguistics expert to be able to explain it all very well but, as I say, it was a political step and a linguistic one, too, subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that before 1989, in the Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, the official language was Croato-Serbian language. Does it have anything to do with the fact that according to the constitution of Croatia in Croatia in addition to the Croatian people, there were also the Serbs? In other words, the Serbs were a people recognised in the constitution and that's why they had to have their own language? Does it have anything to do with it or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, there is something to it but not that much. The name of the language was such because it was one language that was spoken by the Croats, Serbs, Muslims, and Montenegrins. It was the technical term for the language in the linguistic literature. This term was used for the language, in Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were various combinations. In Croatia it was called Croato-Serbian in Serbia it was called Serbo-Croatian and in Bosnia-Herzegovina it was called Serbo-Croatian/Croato-Serbian or alternatively Croato-Serbian/Serbo-Croatian what it all boiled down to was that this was the language of Croats, Serbs, Muslims, and Montenegrins, and it was the one and only language and in that sense, the term was coined in order to establish the relationship between the language and the peoples. And in Croatia, as to the existence of Serbs and Croats as peoples in the constitution, that does have some indirect link with the name of the language but it's a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If before 1989 the official language in Croatia was Croato-Serbian language and after the changes that took place in 1989, the official language was the Croatian literary language, did that imply that the Serbian language was rejected from the official use?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1989, as I've already explained, this very peculiar wording was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's not dwell upon that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first changing in the name and then in 1990 under the HDZ, the term Serbian was completely erased from the name of the language and I believe that this is what you want me to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did this second change in the name of the language take place, the one that was carried out by the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in June or rather the beginning of July 1990, and it was incorporated into the -- into draft amendments to the constitution of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did this happen after the first multi-party elections in Croatia in April 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During the first multi-party elections in 1990, was it the HDZ that won the first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the HDZ had 41 per cent of the total number of votes at the multi-party elections but owing to the majority system, it got the majority of seats in the parliament of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the president of the HDZ, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, became the president of the Republic of Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He became the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Croatia, which meant the head of state, yes, in the sense that you're asking me, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the introduction of the Croatian language as the official language of Croatia, were there any other changes introduced in terms of the status of the Serbian people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about those changes that were introduced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few changes that had an indirect or direct impact on the Serbian people in Croatia. One of those changes was the abolition of the association of municipalities, which was interpreted as an attack on the right of Serbs, although in direct terms this could not be implied. However in the assembly this was the consequence of that change. You have already mentioned the change in the name of the language, and then the constituent nature of the Serbian people was also changed so the status of the Serbian people who from then on were treated as a national minority. The symbols of the state were introduced in terms of -- in order to underline the ethnic symbols of Croatia, the change in the name of the republic, which did not have any consequence or impact on the interethnic relationship. The word socialist was erased from the name of the state because this was in line with the reforms that were taking place in society. Those were the draft amendments to the constitution which were proposed towards the end of June and the beginning of July 1990. Finally everything was implemented in the new constitution that was passed in December 1990, the new constitution of Croatia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have spoken in great detail about these changes, Mr. Babic, and you said amongst other things that a -- mono-ethnic symbols of the state were introduced as ethnic symbols of the state. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chequerboard was introduced and the chequerboard is a customary term for the Croatian historical coat of arms which until then was only one part of the coat of arms of the Republic of Croatia, which also featured the five-pointed star. However, after the changes, the chequerboard was featured on its own, without any additions, and it represented a historical symbol of the Croatian state and the Croatian people. However, it provoked discussions, both amongst the Croats as well as amongst the Serbs, as to the meaning of this chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this chequerboard in any way connected with the independent state of Croatia which existed between the years 1941 and 1945 and what it meant then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, it provoked discussions and it evoked the Independent State of Croatia when a similar symbol was the symbol of the independent state of Croatia. There was a lot of discussion among the general public in Croatia as to what was the symbol of the independent state of Croatia and what was the symbol of the Republic of Croatia, and it all boiled down to the distribution of fields, the red field and the white field, and the layout of the chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the main political goal of the party led by Mr. Tudjman was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the democratisation of society, the break-up with the communist past, nationalist and expansionist political goal as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What in your view was the nationalist goal and what did it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, it meant the so-called Croatisation of this, that and the other, all the public institutions started being called Croatian, not in terms of the Republic of Croatia as such but it was rather an ethnic determination. We have already spoken about the structure, the changes in the names and the introduction of the so-called "new-speak" into the political language, and the language in the society, and also there was a new political programme that went for the creation of a confederation or ultimately the creation of an Independent State of Croatia. At least during the election campaign of the president of the party, Mr. Tudjman, this state should have incorporated parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned Bosnia and Herzegovina and the political goal that relates to Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would like to tell you that we will go back to that later on but now let me ask you this: In order to sum up whatever happened during this very short period of time in the first half of the year 1990, could you say that the constitutional changes meant that the Serbs lost their status of a nation in Croatia, that they lost their language, that they lost a possibility to organise their association of municipalities that had existed in the constitution until then, that they lost their own symbols and that they had to accept Croatian symbols and that the main Croatian symbol was the same chequerboard that was the symbol of the independent state of Croatia that was the execution ground of many a Serb during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything save for the shape of the chequerboard. It did remind of the chequerboard that was used during the Independent State of Croatia. However, an explanation that was given was that the Ustasha chequerboard started with a white field, whereas the real, the genuine, historical one started with a red field. So my answer would be yes, with this little reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did all these changes that took place in the political life of Croatia and that concerned the Serbian people in Croatia, were they all announced and were they announced by the notorious sentence used by Mr. Tudjman at the founding meeting of the Croatian Democratic Union, who said, and I quote, "The independent state of Croatia, the fascist, quisling creation of Croatia was not only a quisling Croatia and a fascist crime but also an expression of historical strive of the Croatian people," do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Tudjman did utter that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The constitutional changes that were introduced through the amendments to the constitution of Croatia, did they meet with the approval of the Serbian people in Croatia or were -- was the Serbian people opposed to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political representatives of the Serbian people opposed those amendments, and this opposition was supported by the Serbian people at their plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what form did this opposition take, the opposition of the representatives of the Serbian people in Croatia, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there were political rallies at which there were discussions on the constitutional amendments. There it was a public debate amongst the representatives of those municipalities where the Serbs constituted a majority, the representatives in the parliament and other public figures discussed those amendments and rejected them. When the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is enough, Mr. Babic. We will come to the topics that you have just tackled. I wanted to ask you something else and I apologise for interrupting you. The fact that the constitution was being changed at the time, was it done according to a procedure? Was it done by way of amendments? Were the constitutional amendments introduced in keeping with the constitution of the Republic of Croatia? I'm talking about the year 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the legality of those amendments is concerned, yes. However, in general terms, in terms of the principles contained in the constitution, my answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What of these amendments was not in keeping with the constitution in terms of the principles contained in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may provide you with the conclusion that the political representatives of Serbs passed at the time, they believed that it was a prevalence or the imposition of the will of one constituent people on another constituent people which was a violation of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This predominance that you're talking about, was it done with very clear symbols, with very clear reference to some symbols from the past, for example, the chequerboard and the new words that were introduced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already spoken about the chequerboard and I -- I've told you about the discussions and the interpretations of that chequerboard amongst the Serb the problem was emphasised especially in the Serbian media, the chequerboard was considered the symbol of the Ustasha state and the Serbs gradually adopted such an interpretation of the chequerboard. On the other hand, I've told you what it represented. It had been part of the coat of arms of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. On its own it was the historical coat of arms of Croatia and the Croats said that because of the distribution of fields, it was not an Ustasha symbol. But what I am trying to tell you is what the reaction of the Serbs was. The Serbs perceived this chequerboard as something that had a link with the Independent State of Croatia. That's how the media interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We've already mentioned that Mr. Franjo Tudjman, at the founding meeting of the Croatian Democratic Union in February 1990 spoke about the independent Croatian state as a historical strife of the Croatian people. Do you know whether the most prominent people from the Ustasha immigration, who had come from abroad, and who had previously been banned from returning to Yugoslavia, were they sitting at that meeting? Were they there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you're talking about the first generally of the HDZ that took place at the time. This was not at the founding meeting of the HDZ or at least not in formal terms. The party already existed and this was the first rally of the HDZ. I don't know who attended that meeting. However, the media, in the media there was news that a lot of political immigrants who had previously not been able to return to Yugoslavia were present at that rally. I don't know who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. When these amendments were introduced, those that concerned the status of the Serbs, the national status of the Serbs in Croatia, the Serbs proposed their objections to the amendments, introducing such changes to the Republic of Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those amendments were rejected because they were perceived as the amendments that violated the constitution and the rights of the Serbian people to be a constituent people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we understood each other properly, Mr. Babic. I just wanted to ask the following. There this kind of constitutional amendment was proposed did the Serbs respond by their counter-amendments and what happened to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a rejection of these amendments and there were proposals that had not been accepted by the commission for preparing a new constitution, the new constitution of Croatia. There were two types of proposals. One had to do with the items on the agenda concerning changes to the constitution, that was the autumn of 1990, and then there was the proposal to establish an autonomous region or district of Krajina within Croatia, but that was rejected by the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to understand what we've just been discussing, can you tell us what the basic tenet of the Yugoslav federal constitution is from 1990? Who led the federal state, the federation? There were the republics and what organs were in the federation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly, the Presidency of the SFRY, the federal executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant, Mr. Babic. Thank you. What about the Presidency of the SFRY? To put it in very simple terms, was that the collective head of state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the members of the Presidency of the collective head of state were in 1990? I'm not asking you about the actual names of the members but what structures did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was one single representative from each republic and autonomous province.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many republics did Yugoslavia have in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many members did the Presidency of Yugoslavia have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how come six republics have eight members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that each republic had a member respectively and then also the two autonomous provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These two provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina, according to the constitution of Yugoslavia from 1974 were where, whose provinces were they, an integral part of what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the territory of Serbia, but they had a dual constitutional position. They were within Serbia and within the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So according to the constitution of 1974, the Republic of Serbia as one of the members of the Yugoslav federation had within it two autonomous provinces that had a very high degree of authority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did any other Yugoslav republic have any autonomous provinces within their composition?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the evidence you've given to date, you've mentioned a great deal, different areas in the former Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, you've mentioned Dalmatia, Kordun, Lika, Banija, Slavonia, Baranja. You even showed us the borders of these area; is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did any of these areas have the status of an autonomous provinces in the sense in which Vojvodina and Kosovo had that status?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As for Vojvodina and Kosovo as parts of Serbia, according to the constitution of Yugoslavia, did they decide on the president of the Presidency of Serbia so without the Kosovo and Vojvodina votes could the president of Serbia be elected?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you've put a question to me that I'm not quite sure of but I can tell you what I know. The election of the members of the Presidency was carried out within the assembly until the new constitution of Serbia was adopted in 1990. Now, I don't know exactly what you meant, which period in mind -- which period of time you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said the Kosovo and Vojvodina as parts of Serbia were members of the Yugoslav federation, too. For example, they gave their own president -- own members for the Presidency of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in the Chamber of republics and provinces in the federal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the representative of Kosovo, otherwise an ethnic Albanian, Fadil Hodza, was the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia in the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during one term of office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this came about? Out of these eight members of the Presidency, one would be the presiding member, the president. What was the mechanism involved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were rules of procedure or a protocol regulating the shifts involved among the presidents -- members of the Presidency who would be president and who would be vice-president, a certain order was set. So for one year, one of the members of the Presidency would carry out the duties of the president of the Presidency, and, of course, another member, one of the members of the Presidency, would be the vice-president of the Presidency. So there was a system of rotation. One of the members of the Presidency would come to this position of president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to make what you've told us just now clearer, in 1990, and before that, did Slovenia have its own member of the Presidency and, if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Slovenia had Drnovsek, Janez Drnovsek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. What about Croatia? Did it have its representative in the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First it was Stipe Suvar, and Mesic was first Prime Minister and then during the course of 1990, I don't know exactly when this happened, but until the end of 1990, Croatia did change its member of the Presidency, Suvar was recalled and Mesic came to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the other republics and these two autonomous provinces, did they all have their respective members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. So the Presidency consisted of eight members and these eight members elected their president of the Presidency, the presiding member; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this question has now been asked several times and it's been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Do you have anything to say? I think we have been going in circles around the same point for a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just trying to get an answer from the witness to my question, my question being whether the constitutional provision from the federal constitution made it possible for every republic, every member of the Yugoslav federation that when its order -- its turn came, according to a certain order, a certain protocol that had been agreed upon previously, that they would get their own president of the Presidency. Did every Yugoslav republic and province have that possibility and then the witness was talking about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That question can be put in a very small and short sentence. You have actually put it before and the witness told you that there was a rotation system in terms of which every republic got an opportunity to be -- to get the president -- the Presidency of the Presidency. You even asked him about Kosovo, which is -- which was then an autonomous region and he said, yes, Kosovo did get an opportunity to get -- to be president of the Presidency. I think you can ask that question one simple sentence and get the answer. We are moving way out of the area of the indictment. We are doing a history of former Yugoslavia, and we haven't got much time. This witness has got only two more days with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, the defence is just trying to get an answer to the question in terms of the thesis put forth by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just put your question to the witness. Let the witness answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not going to comment the charges made by the Prosecution in terms of the political situation in Yugoslavia, but I put these questions in order to get some answers in this respect. However, now you started a question that actually confused me, totally. So far, we have not had any information as to how long the cross-examination of this witness would last. This witness is the most important Prosecution witness that is to appear here and he was examined for more than four days. I think that the remaining two days that you refer to are absolutely inappropriate for the Defence and that the Defence has to raise a great many other important issues. This has just been an introduction to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might address that, this was something I was going to raise with Defence counsel after today's session and try to address it with the Chamber outside of Court so as not to use up court time but now that it's come up, the Court is, of course, referring to the fact that the witness is scheduled to finish at the end of the week of -- on March 3rd, for other reasons, and that's how it's been scheduled. However, that schedule was made contemplating that we would be sitting additional days. And now that we have this gap of one week, I do think that we should address whether the witness could be held over a little bit longer so that the Defence has adequate time to cross-examine the witness. And that was something I was going to ask the Defence counsel how long he anticipated needing and then raise with the Court whether the witness could be kept perhaps an additional day or two so the cross-examination could be finished. Having said that, I do think that the cross-examination so far has gone quite afield on some areas and if there is some way that it could be moved a little more quickly. But I'd leave that to the Chamber to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine on the first point, Mr. Whiting, if what has happened before can be taken as precedent, if you do want the witness to stay a little longer, you do that by motion, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was my intention, and I'll take care of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. So there is no need to either discuss it with the Chamber or with the Defence outside court. You can just do that by motion. You can discuss it with the Defence to find out how long they are going to be with him in order for you to determine how long you would like him to be here for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was my intention, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. On the second point, this is not the first time the Court has indicated that, in fact, the cross-examination is going afield, and we've been trying to get Mr. Milovancevic to at least come back to the issues of this case. I once again say so to you, Mr. Milovancevic. I do not want to restrict you in your cross-examination of the witness, but I think it is important to stay relevant. We've been irrelevant in terms of time, we've dealt with 1971, some 20 years prior to the period relevant to this case. We are now talking about the constitution of the Presidency of the SFRY. This witness has indicated in one sentence that there was a rotational system in terms of which each of the republics and the autonomous regions, the two autonomous regions got an opportunity to become president of the Presidency. I'm not quite sure what else we need. But if there is anything else you need, by all means, get to it and let's get to it as fast as we possibly can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate what you've said, Your Honour, and I shall always go by your words, and honour them. I just wanted to say that the Defence tried to indicate a highly relevant fact, namely that the efforts to destroy Yugoslavia, which in 1990 was the only internationally recognised entity, did not start in February, 1989, but a lot before that, 20 years before that. So what happened in 1990 was just a finale of a long process where one has to view the roles of all the protagonists involved, their true and concealed objectives, in order to draw a conclusion as to what actually happened on the scene, on the political scene in Yugoslavia. I'm sorry to have burdened the Trial Chamber with so many facts that have to do with the previous period, but this is just a sketch of what happened beforehand and what finally exploded in 1991. Throughout these proceedings, we have been talking about Croatia, about the JNA, about its role as an aggressor, the Defence is just trying to point out one detail: The only international legal entity in 1990 was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia as a subject of international law. In order to understand what was going on and what the true causes were and what were the consequences and effects only, I guess I went into quite a bit of detail but I tried to give you a full picture. May I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did go into quite a bit of detail and you haven't told us one wit about what Mr. Martic did from 1971 to 1990. And this court is here about Mr. Martic, and we haven't heard one word about what he did from 1971. Yes, please go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic. Let us get on with the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since this is cross-examination, as for the role of Mr. Martic in this period, the Defence is going to talk about that when we reach a stage in these proceedings when that is our objective. Now we are only responding to what was put another by the Prosecution during examination in chief. I shall move on to my question straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, what was the factual consequence of the decision to get rid of the Serbs as a people, as a nation, from the Croatian constitution, indeed what was the legal effect of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what is your question? You have two there, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me be more precise. You say that the Croatian parliament adopted the amendments and threw out the Serbs from the constitution of Croatia as a nation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very specific. I said that on the 25th of July 1991, the Croatian parliament adopted the proposed amendments to the Croatian constitution and in the month of December, perhaps I'm not going to get the date exactly right, but I think it was the 23rd of December maybe, when it adopted the new constitution of the Republic of Croatia, in which the Serbs were no longer treated as a constituent peoples, nation, but were reduced to the concept of a national minority, if that was what you meant by your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The right of political assertion and the position of Croatia as a member of the Yugoslav federation, could the Serbs have that right when they were reduced to a national minority, this right of expression, political expression?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question was opened up in April and May 1991, in the following sense or rather in the sense that you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The status of a state, and this was pursuant to an agreement of the presidents of the republic that met and the crisis that escalated at that time. So could you tell me what period you mean? What period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Mr. Babic, you said that the Serbian Democratic Party started dealing with issues which were vital to the Serb population in Croatia, and then you said that the amendments to the Croatian constitution were rejected; is that right? When was that and who did that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Croatian parliament or rather the assembly of the Serbian people in Croatia held on the 25th of July 1991, the amendments were rejected to the Croatian constitution which delved into the question of constituent nationality of the Serbs in Croatia. Is that what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that in the 25th of July and was it held in the town called Srb and who attended that rally and was a decision passed or that assembly meeting? When -- what were the decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 100.000 citizens of Serb ethnicity from the Republic of Croatia territory took part in that assembly. What was your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were any other political representatives of the Serb people who attended?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were representatives of the democratic party, the Yugoslav independent democratic party, representatives of the Serbian Orthodox Church, and individuals, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was all that in 1990, the 25th of July 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Because in the transcript, it says 1991. So there was an omission there. It was 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the basic decisions of that declaration were, the declaration that was adopted? What were the decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The declaration was adopted rejecting the constitutional amendments to the constitution of Croatia which denied the status of the Serb nation as a nation on a footing of equality with the other nations in Croatia, and the declaration also determined and ascertained that the constitutional amendment relating to rescinding the communality of municipalities be rejected. The declaration also speaks about strivings towards a possible or rather the declaration assumes future relations in Yugoslavia and the way in which the national rights of the Serbs in Croatia would be realised and it was said and decided that if Yugoslavia remains a federation, the Serb nation, the Serb people, are called for territorial -- would call for territorial autonomy or self-government, and if Yugoslavia was structured and organised as a confederation of states, then the Serb people would ask for political territorial autonomy within the frameworks of the Republic of Croatia. So that -- well, you have the text of the declaration itself if you wish to discuss it further. You can refer to the actual declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would be a good idea to place on the overhead projector and on our screens, the declaration of the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people of the 25th of June 1990 and it is found in tab -- the number is 02141952, 02141953. ERN number, that is. And I think it was Exhibit 141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say that you want that on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please have it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told it can be put on e-court. May we please have it on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Exhibit 141 and I think that we could see it on the e-court, yes. We have the declaration on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read out what it says? It is in B/C/S or the Serb language. And there is an English version as well. Can you read point 1 of the declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Within the borders of the socialist Republic of Croatia which is the state of the Serb people as well, living in the socialist Republic of Croatia, the Serb nation on the basis of its geographical, historical, social and cultural characteristics is a sovereign nation with all the rights contained in the sovereignty of nations." Do you want me to read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just dwell there for a moment. Let's stop there for a moment. That first paragraph of Article 1, point 1, does it refer to the Serb people within the borders of Croatia? Is that something that is not challenged? We are talking about the Serb people living within the borders of the Republic of Croatia, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what does it say? Would you read on, read the next paragraph for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Serb people in the socialist Republic of Croatia has the full right of joining in communality with the Croatian people or independently in establishing new relationships in Yugoslavia should -- may decide either for a federative or confederal state organisation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Read the next paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With no forms of Yugoslav communality can be elected without the participation of the Serb people, and this is particularly true for -- in situations of a legitimate secession. Nations are seceded, not states, nations can secede, not states."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. These quotes from this declaration on the autonomy of the Serb people, are they in conformity with the provisions of the Croatian constitution and Yugoslav constitution? Is there anything there that would be contrary to positive Yugoslav law, law positive, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already spoken about that. I said that the Serbs and Serb political representatives of that time interpreted the principles of the Croatian constitution. This was interpreting with those principles. Now as far as the principles and concept of who had the right to secede, whether it was the republics or the people, that was a debatable issue at that time. The Serbs accepted this concept advocated by Milosevic and the socialist party and the leadership of Serbia, which met in September and was expounded by Abedisa Borojevic [phoen], that it was the nations that had the right to self-determination regardless of republican borders, and this related to that particular position and concept and its acceptance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read out the next provision, point 2 of the declaration? The entire point?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the basis of its sovereignty, the Serb people in Croatia have the right to autonomy. The contents of that autonomy will depend on the federal or confederal setup of Yugoslavia. Under conditions of a federal state setup the Serb people have the right to unimpeded and limitless use of the Serbian literary language in official and private use, the Cyrillic script in schools and Serbian school programmes, and that's where my text ends here. I see nothing further on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Turn to the next page of that same document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It continues: "Cultural and political institutions, enterprises, the press and Serb radio and television. An organisation of this type of autonomy can be implemented only through full municipal self-government, especially in the municipalities where the Serbs make up the majority and by linking up those municipalities within a community under conditions of a confederative state setup of Yugoslavia, the Serb people in Croatia have the right to political, territorial autonomy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Now, in that point 2 of the declaration, according to that point by this political act, are the Serb people in Croatia called upon to realise their constitutional rights which existed up until then for them as a nation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of point 2, do we see which rights the Serb people have under a federal state setup? Is that what is stipulated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or the rights required or demanded, yes, for the realisation of those rights, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these right, the rights mentioned in paragraph 2, the right to use the Serbian literary language, the right to use the Cyrillic alphabet, the right to have schools and Serbian school programmes, the right to their political and cultural institutions, the right to their own enterprises, press and Serb radio, television, were those rights enjoyed by the Serb people at that time in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could the Serb people realise those rights on the basis of municipal self-government which is referred to in paragraph 3, especially in those municipalities where the Serbs were the majority population and by the linking up of those municipalities into a community?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the optimum way in which those right could be realised and enjoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Requirements and demands of this kind, democratic -- basic human rights, in fact, are being stressed by the Serb people at a point in time where the amendments to the Croatian constitution are just about to be adopted in which the Serb people are being eradicated from the constitution, where the Serbian language is being thrown out of the constitution, at which point in time they are -- local self-government is being made impossible through the community of municipalities because they too are being pushed out of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in point 2, does it mention autonomy and then provide for two options, one variant would be within a federal state and the second option would be within a confederal state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the possibilities. These are the options. And solutions under supposed conditions, assumed conditions, of that kind, because solutions of that kind were already up for discussion within Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the then leadership of Croatia, led by Franjo Tudjman, spoke about a future confederal setup for Yugoslavia or an independent Croatia, is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the last paragraph of this declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people, does it say that or rather the last point in point 2, that under a confederative state setup the Serb people in Croatia would have the right to political territorial autonomy, is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This last paragraph, then, is that an answer or response to possible political options to which the new leadership of Croatia was aspiring, conducting the constitutional amendments that we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in points 3, 4 and 5 of this declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people, does it say who the political representative the Serb people in Croatia is to be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, those political representatives of the Serb people in Croatia pursuant to this declaration, are they the Serb Sabor or assembly meeting in Srb whose executive organ is the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In point 4 does it say the following, that the Serb National Council has the right to organise plebiscite -- a plebiscite for the Serb people to state their views on all questions of vital interest to their position in Croatia and Yugoslavia, as well as other issues having to do with the realisation of Serb sovereignty and autonomy?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does point 6 of this declaration state that this Serb Sabor or assembly at its session in Srb on the 25th of July 1990 proclaims null and void for the Serb people in Croatia all constitutional and other legal amendments denying its sovereignty as a nation and diminish their autonomous rights?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Up until that time, did the Croatian Sabor or assembly, had it already rejected all the Serb amendments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On that day, the assembly met in Zagreb, on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On that same day, the assembly met in Zagreb, and what was the topic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the adoption of the constitutional amendments, that was on the agenda. Now, what I want to say is this: That was a response to the meeting of the Croatian parliament to pass the amendments to the constitution that we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that by adopting this declaration, the representatives of the Serb people in Croatia just tried to ward off the negative consequences that would emerge from a change in the Croatian constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or rather let me be more precise. They wanted to protect their rights under the principles of the constitution that was in force until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Now, point 7 of the declaration, does it say the following that the Serb people in Croatia are seeking nothing more than the right that is other modern nations in Europe have had for a long time and are enjoying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This assembly in Srb, in terms of its content and in terms of its mode of operation, did it constitute any kind of extremist national behaviour on the part of the people present or was this a struggle for vital national rights?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's two questions. It did not constitute extremist nationalist behaviour. Rather, as interpreted in the public, as well, or rather as I interpreted its function, it was the second half, the other half, of the parliament of Croatia, because one half, not an exact laugh in terms of numbers, was in session in Zagreb at that time. This was the other half, consisting of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Serb National Council? It was the executive organ of the Croatian Sabor. Did it act in accordance with paragraph 4 of this declaration, namely organise a plebiscite of the Serb people in Croatia with regard to all questions that are relevant to their status?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When was this done and how was this carried through?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb National Council were elected by the assembly in Srb. It was constituted on the 31st of July 1991. At this first session a decision was reached to organise a referendum. The legal grounds for this were not specified. It was just stated that a plebiscite or a referendum of the Serb people would be organised until the legal grounds for carrying out the plebiscite were established. At the second meeting of the Serb National Council on the 16th of August, in Dvor Na Uni, a decision was adopted for that announced referendum or plebiscite would be carried out in accordance with the constitutions of Croatia and Yugoslavia and relevant laws and that it would not be called a referendum but it would be called an expression of views in accordance with the Croatian constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you say when the Serb people in Croatia expressed their views in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 17th of August 1990, until the 2nd of September 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I ask, in the answer before, Mr. Babic, you said 31st of July 1991. This also is 1990, I suppose.
